results.term_definition: Gemini is one of the 13 constellations of the Zodiac and one of the 88 modern constellations as accepted by the International Astronomical Union, but goes back much further – it was already one of the 48 constellations named by the 2nd century astronomer Claudius Ptolemy. The constellation gets its name from its two brightest stars Castor and Pollux, who in Babylonian mythology were twins and minor gods. Gemini is visible in the northern hemisphere during winter, located between the constellations Taurus and Cancer. Various cultures around the world have their own stories associated with this constellation and its stars. Castor and Pollux are located approximately 50 and 30 light years from Earth, respectively. About 80 stars may be seen in Gemini with the naked eye. Some notable deep-sky objects located within the region of this constellation are M35, NGC 2158, NGC 2392, and Abell 21.
